Audio System One Model: Typed Probabilistic
Perception of Emotion in Speech

Jaime Bellver-Soler    Iván Martín-Fernández    Anmol Guragain    Luis Fernando D’Haro
Abstract

Speech applications ask many questions about the same voice: which emotion a listener perceives, how aroused the speaker sounds, whether they sound frustrated. Classifiers answer fast, over one fixed label set; audio language models (ALMs) take any question in text, but answer by generation, one pass per question, with poorly calibrated probabilities. We present ASOM (Audio System One Model), a System One model for speech: choice, score and yes/no questions written at request time are answered in one pass, without generation, each with a probability distribution. Frozen speech and text encoders feed a 6.2M-parameter reader with no per-class parameters, trained on listener vote distributions. On MSP-Podcast, ASOM matches a classifier on the same features and data, leads the best of 6 zero-shot ALMs by 0.072 and an ALM fine-tuned on the same data by 0.026, and answers 20 questions in 13.1 ms, 17–41 times faster than the ALMs. It also answers reworded, reduced and new label sets, scales and gender, and on 21 unseen corpora in 13 languages it leads the best zero-shot ALM by 0.138 where the words carry no emotion; where they do, the ALMs mostly read.

Index Terms: 
System One models, zero-shot classification, speech emotion recognition, audio language models, calibration

1 Introduction

Voice agents, call-centre analytics and content moderation ask many questions about the same clip, and a deployed system usually fixes its questions, or a decision tree over them, in advance. Two families of models serve them, at opposite ends of a trade-off (Fig. 1). Speech classifiers [12] are fast and calibrated, but a new emotion word, a coarser label set or a new attribute needs a new model. Audio language models (ALMs) [14, 33] take any question in text, but answer by generation: each question costs a prefill, the implied probability is poorly calibrated, and they trail supervised models on emotion [40].

A third kind of model sits between the two: describe each label in words and score the input against that description, as zero-shot classifiers of text, images and audio have long done (Sec. 2). TypeSafe recently named such models System One models [2], after Kahneman’s fast, intuitive System 1 [23]: a request carries typed questions (a choice over described options, an ordinal score, a yes/no proposition), each answered by a calibrated distribution in one pass, at the latency of a small classifier. Their model, Jev, reads text only.

We present ASOM, a System One model for speech: given a clip and questions written in text, it returns one probability distribution per question. It is not a classifier with a fixed label set, since questions and options are written at request time, nor an ALM, since it is not an autoregressive generative model, nor a contrastive model: each option becomes a text, a criterion, scored against one audio vector, and the model is trained to reproduce the listeners’ distribution of answers rather than to rank captions. Because the labels are text, the same model can be asked a reduced or reworded label set, new emotion words, an emotion scale or another attribute such as gender, without retraining; this instance is trained on listener judgements of affect. The cost does not depend on the number of questions, and the criteria, independent of the audio, are cached: a deployment with fixed questions pays only for the speech encoder. Our contributions:

  • •

    ASOM11 1 Code and model weights will be publicly released upon acceptance. This work has been submitted to the ICASSP for possible publication. (Sec. 3): a 6.2M-parameter reader with no per-class parameters over frozen speech and text encoders, trained on listener vote distributions.

  • •

    A comparison on MSP-Podcast (Sec. 5.1) with classifiers trained on the same data, six zero-shot ALMs, a fine-tuned ALM and three CLAP models, on the same clips.

  • •

    Tests of what a classifier cannot do (Secs. 5.2–5.3): reworded, reduced and new label sets, scales, gender and 21 unseen corpora, with a transcript-only control separating hearing from reading.

2 Related Work

Speech emotion classifiers put a fixed-class head on a pretrained speech encoder [12, 18], the strongest adding text streams over an ASR transcript [11]. Training on listener vote distributions instead of majority labels [3, 13] captures how listeners disagree; ASOM keeps this supervision, but each class is a text, not an output unit.

Contrastive audio–text models (CLAP) score a clip against any text [32]: MS-CLAP covers speech emotion among 16 zero-shot tasks [17], paralinguistic models train on emotion captions [21] or smoothed targets [22], and WavLink scores question–option texts against a Whisper token [24]. ASOM shares their dual-encoder shape, but they return similarities learned from captions or consensus labels, not calibrated answers learned from listener votes.

Audio LLMs take any question, but trail specialised models on emotion [40]; fine-tuning them towards annotator distributions [38] keeps a fixed label set and a billion-parameter decoder.

Labels as text and System One models. Scoring written labels without generation is much older than its current name: dataless classification embedded label names [10], entailment classifiers test each label as a yes/no hypothesis [37], encoders score all the written options of a question in one pass [36] or several label sets at once [39], and dual encoders carried the idea to images [28] and to audio, speech emotion included [16, 34]. TypeSafe named the class System One models and popularised a typed request with Jev [2], a text-only model with no paper. Two concurrent audio prototypes [4, 5] use neither listener votes nor shared benchmarks.

3 Audio System One Model

Fig. 2 shows ASOM: two frozen encoders turn the audio and the text of each option into vectors, and a small trained reader compares them and returns one probability distribution per question.

Requests and criteria. A request is one clip and a list of typed questions in JSON format [2]: a choice picks one of several options (e.g., which emotion is heard), a score picks a level of an ordered scale (e.g., arousal from 1 to 7), and a yes/no question asks whether a statement holds (e.g., is the speaker female?). Each option is written as one text, a criterion: the question followed by the option’s name and a short description (Fig. 2). A choice question gives one criterion per option, a score one per level, and a yes/no question two.

Encoders. A frozen Qwen2.5-1.5B [35] processes each criterion: the layer-normalised mean of its output token states is the criterion vector cjc_{j}, which does not depend on the audio and is cached. The frozen Whisper-large-v3 [29] encodes the clip and from four of its 32 transformer blocks (8, 16, 24 and 32) we take the mean over the clip and the means of 64 time segments. A learned softmax mixes the four blocks, four learned queries attend over the segments, and their output is added to the clip mean through a zero-initialised gate, giving the audio vector aa. If the request includes a transcript, a second frozen text encoder, RoBERTa-large, encodes it into one more input next to aa.

Reader. Two small heads map both vectors to ℝ256\mathbb{R}^{256} and scale them to unit length: c^j=Wc​cj/∥Wc​cj∥\hat{c}_{j}=W_{c}c_{j}/\lVert W_{c}c_{j}\rVert and a^=h/∥h∥\hat{a}=h/\lVert h\rVert, with h=GELU⁡(Wa​LN​(a))h=\mathrm{GELU}(W_{a}\,\mathrm{LN}(a)). Because both have unit norm, their dot product already is their cosine similarity, with no division by the norms, and option jj gets

sj=τ​c^j⊤​a^+b⁡(c^j),p⁡(j)=esj/∑k∈Qesk,s_{j}=\tau\,\hat{c}_{j}^{\top}\hat{a}+b(\hat{c}_{j}),\qquad p(j)=e^{s_{j}}\big/\textstyle\sum_{k\in Q}e^{s_{k}}, (1)

where τ=8\tau=8 is fixed, bb, a linear function of the criterion alone, learns how often each option is chosen in training, and the softmax runs over the options QQ of the question. A score also returns its expected level, and a yes/no question the probability of its affirmative criterion. A request’s criteria are all scored in one matrix product (63 criteria for 20 questions in 0.6 ms), so the cost barely depends on how many questions; removing options renormalises the rest.

Training. Each question’s target is the distribution of listeners’ answers [3]: the share picking each option, a score’s rating histogram, or the share answering yes. The loss is the cross-entropy to this distribution (the log score, a strictly proper scoring rule), so the reader learns how listeners disagree, not only their majority.

With few listeners per clip, these targets are noisy, so the reader also learns from a smoother one, built by cross-fitting: the training clips are split into disjoint folds, auxiliary readers are trained on all folds but one, and each predicts only the clips of the fold it never saw. Averaged per clip, these predictions form an ensemble estimate of the listeners’ answers; ensembles are better calibrated than single models [25], and distilling one into a single model retains much of that gain at the cost of one model [20]. Because no auxiliary reader saw the clip it predicts, the target does not simply copy that clip’s votes. The loss adds the cross-entropy to this target to the one to the votes; the final model is still one reader, and without this step its log loss worsens (Sec. 5.4). Only the reader is trained; the encoders remain frozen.

4 Experimental Setup

Training data. Learning from votes needs corpora that release each listener’s answer. Most emotion corpora give one label per clip, usually the emotion an actor was asked to portray, which says nothing of how listeners disagree; we keep them for testing. We train on three corpora that release individual votes, each with its own label set: MSP-Podcast 2.0 [7] (Train, 169k podcast clips with each listener’s primary and secondary emotions and 7-point arousal, valence and dominance), CREMA-D [8] (acted English, 6–12 listeners per clip) and the Italian Emozionalmente [9] (5 per clip).

Training. Each clip is asked four questions, with targets from the annotations: its primary emotion; arousal, valence, and dominance (the histogram of 7-point ratings); gender; and yes/no per emotion. Half of the steps paraphrase the questions and options, so the reader does not learn one wording. Cross-fitting (Sec. 3) uses 32 auxiliary readers (disjoint folds, several seeds each); results average three seeds.

Evaluation data. The main benchmark is MSP-Podcast 2.0 Dev-select (28,759 clips, 553 speakers), a speaker-disjoint development partition used for model selection. As the ALMs are slow, all systems answer the same speaker-stratified subset of 3,113 clips (Table 1; on all 28,759, they score within the same intervals) and a nested 1,000-clip subset (Table 2). For transfer, we take up to 1,200 clips from each of 21 corpora unseen by ASOM (20,585 clips, 13 languages, acted and natural, 3–10 labels, 17 from EmoBox [27]), each asked with its own labels; ten give speaker gender (10,011 clips). EmoNet-Voice Bench [31] (4,560 synthetic clips, 38 emotions) and EARS [30] (2,760 clips, 23 emotions) add emotions outside every training label set.

Baselines. Divided in three families:

  • •

    Classifiers, trained by us on MSP-Podcast: fine-tuned WavLM-large [12], an MLP on CLAP’s HTSAT audio encoder [32] and DeepSER, the four-stream block (WavLM, Whisper and two text encoders over its own transcript) of MEDUSA [11]; plus emotion2vec+ large [18] off the shelf.

  • •

    Audio LLMs, zero-shot: Qwen2.5-Omni 3B and 7B [33], Qwen2-Audio-7B-Instruct [14], Audio Flamingo 3 [19], Phi-4-multimodal [1] and Voxtral-Mini-3B [26]. They get ASOM’s question and option texts with lettered options, and we read the probabilities of the answer tokens instead of decoding. Omni-3B is also fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 16) on 20k and on all 169k Train clips with ASOM’s targets.

  • •

    CLAP: ParaCLAP [21], MS-CLAP 2023 [17] and LAION CLAP [32].

Metrics. MSP-Podcast: 8-class macro-F1 against the majority label; LL8 against the votes; CCC for arousal, valence and dominance; ROC-AUC for yes/no. Other corpora: macro-F1 on each corpus’s labels, averaged over all unseen corpora (All) or those whose transcript is at chance (Voice); accuracy for gender. Cost: latency of 20 questions on a 5.9 s clip (warm median, one RTX 6000 Ada). Intervals: 95% speaker-clustered bootstrap [6]; differences paired.

5 Results

5.1 Emotion recognition on MSP-Podcast

Table 1 compares all systems on the same clips. ASOM (F1 0.383) is above every audio-only classifier; only DeepSER, which adds two text streams over its own transcript, is ahead (+0.017); an earlier ASOM reader given a transcript as an extra input reaches 0.402. Every other open-label system trails ASOM: the best zero-shot ALM, Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, by 0.072, ParaCLAP by 0.099, and Omni-3B fine-tuned with LoRA on all 169k Train clips by 0.026; the general-audio MS-CLAP and LAION CLAP are near chance (0.112 and 0.077) and left out of Table 1. The probabilities differ even more: every zero-shot ALM has a log loss above the class prior (2.097 or more, against 1.863), so a constant answer is closer to the listeners’ votes, while ASOM is well below it (1.507).

Fig. 1 adds the cost. ASOM answers twenty questions in 13.1 ms, as fast as one, since all criteria are scored in one reader call; most of it is the Whisper encoder (10.6 ms). An ALM runs its language model for each question: even with the audio prefix shared, twenty questions take 230–545 ms, 17–41 times ASOM. CLAP models are also flat and cheaper (ParaCLAP 7.8 ms), but less accurate. A new question also runs the text encoder once (129 ms for twenty, still below the fastest ALM); its criteria are then cached.

5.2 Beyond a fixed label set

A classifier answers only the label set it was trained on. ASOM takes its labels as text, so the same model can be asked what it was never trained to answer; Table 2 tests this against the systems that can do the same, on the MSP-Podcast subset (left) and on corpora that none of them saw in training (right, Sec. 5.3). When every emotion is renamed with a synonym and every description is paraphrased (Syn.), ASOM’s F1 is 0.360 (-0.038 vs. Trained), still the best of the column, ahead of the fine-tuned ALM (0.349). When the question itself is replaced by a new one (New q.), its F1 is 0.363 (-0.035), again the best of the column; no zero-shot ALM exceeds 0.312 in any column.

New emotions can also be added. Asked, as yes/no questions, about eight emotions that were never among its training labels (Words), ASOM reaches an AUC of 0.714 against the listeners’ secondary votes, close to the 0.762 it reaches on the trained emotions and on par with the best zero-shot ALM (0.720); only the fine-tuned ALM is higher (0.760). A classifier cannot be asked these questions at all. The same model also answers scales: asked for arousal, valence and dominance on a 1–7 scale, it reaches a CCC of 0.674, 0.735 and 0.584, while the best of the other systems reaches 0.534, 0.701 and 0.311. Options can also be removed: since each is scored on its own, ASOM simply renormalises over the rest, which an ALM, reading all options together, does not guarantee. Finally, gender, asked in a wording not seen in training, reaches an accuracy of 0.873 on ten corpora, below Omni-7B (0.927).

5.3 Unseen corpora: hearing or reading

On the 21 corpora that ASOM never saw (Table 2, right), ASOM reaches a mean macro-F1 of 0.433, against 0.313 for the best zero-shot ALM and 0.402 for the fine-tuned one. Only emotion2vec+ is higher (0.667), but it was fine-tuned on EmoBox, which holds 17 of these corpora; on the other four the two are close.

Do the ALMs hear the emotion or read it? From the transcript alone, Omni-7B keeps 84% of its F1 on MSP-Podcast (0.261 of 0.311). On the 4 unseen corpora whose sentences reveal the emotion, the best ALM leads ASOM (0.550 vs. 0.494); on the other 17, mostly acted with fixed sentences, the transcript is at chance and ASOM is almost 50% above the best ALM (0.419 vs. 0.281). The ALMs mostly read, as on emotionally incongruent speech [15]; ASOM hears. Emotions outside every training set tell the same story: on EmoNet-Voice and EARS, whose scripts name the emotion, Omni-7B leads but keeps most of it from the transcript alone. ASOM ranks these labels sensibly (AUC 0.721) but seldom chooses them (F1 0.018), because its learned bias bb favours the trained labels.

5.4 Ablations

We reached this design by changing one part at a time, paired against the recipe on Whisper’s fixed 30 s window. Audio: Whisper-large-v3 beats WavLM-large and the audio tower of Qwen2.5-Omni (F1 -0.021 and -0.021). Its deepest blocks matter (stopping at block 24 changes F1 by -0.056), and so do the earlier ones (block 32 alone changes the unseen mean by -0.012); without the time segments F1 changes by -0.022, while one query instead of four changes the unseen mean by only +0.003. Window: the shortest 10, 20 or 30 s window instead of 30 s cuts the 20-question latency from 24.1 to 13.1 ms at the same MSP-Podcast F1, changing the unseen mean by -0.009; no padding at all changes it by -0.047: short clips need Whisper’s padding. Text: a class table in place of the criteria, one learned vector per class as in a classifier, on the same features and data, keeps F1 (0.379 vs. 0.382) and LL8 (1.502 vs. 1.506) but lowers the unseen mean from 0.433 to 0.417 (below ASOM on 16 of 21 corpora): describing the classes in text costs no accuracy and helps transfer. The descriptions matter more than the names: asked with the eight names alone, ASOM’s F1 on the clips of Table 2 falls by -0.063 (to 0.335). The token mean beats the last token on held-out wordings (log loss +0.025). Training: without distillation LL8 worsens by +0.019, without paraphrases the held-out-wording log loss by +0.078, and without CREMA-D and Emozionalmente the unseen mean falls from 0.440 to 0.362. Objective: CLIP’s contrastive loss on label captions instead of the votes changes F1 by -0.053, LL8 by +0.369 and yes/no AUC from 0.763 to 0.596, but raises the unseen mean by +0.067: votes buy calibrated, typed answers; a prior-free objective transfers better.

6 Conclusion

We asked whether a speech model can take its questions in text and still answer like a classifier: in one pass, with calibrated probabilities. ASOM shows that it can. Twenty typed questions cost little more than the speech encoder (13.1 ms). On MSP-Podcast it matches a classifier on the same features and data, so describing the classes in words costs no accuracy, and it is more accurate, better calibrated and 17–41 times cheaper than six zero-shot ALMs; an ALM fine-tuned on the same 169k clips still trails it in accuracy. What a classifier cannot do, ASOM does with the same weights: synonyms, paraphrases or a new question cost it under 0.04 of F1, eight emotion words unseen in training reach an AUC of 0.714, and on 21 unseen corpora in 13 languages it is the best open-label system, almost 50% above the best zero-shot ALM where the words carry no emotion.

The limits are as clear. These are closed tests on affect, and an ALM can be asked much that we did not test: who is speaking, what the question refers to, what else is in the recording. ASOM answers only what its data covers, three corpora with listener votes, all about affect: labels outside them are ranked well (AUC 0.721) but seldom chosen, gender trails Omni-7B, and where the words carry the emotion a transcript still matters. Data is the bottleneck, not the interface, since nothing in the reader is tied to emotion. Our next steps are more data and a larger model: multi-rater corpora in more languages and attributes, and an architecture scaled to any typed question about a recording, to meet the ALMs one to one on every category, not only emotion.

7 Compliance with Ethical Standards

We use public corpora under their licenses and collect no new data. The estimates describe how listeners judge a voice, not the speaker’s internal state, and should not drive high-stakes decisions.
